Hi Emma — thanks for outlining this. Attaching a draft exit checklist and a short summary of the cryptographic sanitization approaches we support. High level answers below; Marissa will follow up with the technical steps and evidence we can provide. Laura, looping you for procurement/SOW wording.

High level:
- Persistent volumes & snapshots: we perform tenant quiesce, remove tenant metadata, delete runtime volumes, and then trigger backend storage secure-delete operations or key destruction depending on the config.
- Backups: we honor the retention policy in the agreement; at exit we either transfer backups to customer custody or irreversibly delete according to the retention/escrow clause.
- Crypto-sanitize options: 1) KMS key deletion (recommended where keys are customer-controlled or dedicated to tenant). 2) Cryptographic rekey/rotate + zeroization of plaintext caches where key destruction is restricted. 3) Physical media wipe procedures for on-prem blades (where applicable).

Hi Emma — quick technical write-up below (concise checklist + evidence items). I included what we do for Redwood-managed KMS vs. customer-managed keys (CMKs).

Summary checklist (tenant decommission):
1) Confirm decommission window and data export requests.
2) Quiesce tenant: stop ingestion jobs, lock write paths.
3) Snapshot & backup handling: either hand off snapshot export (if requested) OR mark for retention=0 and schedule deletion. Document snapshot IDs and deletion timestamps.
4) Persistent volume destruction: delete logical volumes, then issue storage backend secure-delete or cryptographic unlink depending on provider. Record operation IDs.
5) KV cache purge: wipe in-memory caches and clear any persisted caches.
6) KMS action (choose one):
   - Customer-managed key (recommended): customer instructs their KMS to schedule/execute key deletion; provide deletion receipt (timestamp + key-id).
   - Redwood-managed key: we perform an HSM-assisted key destroy flow and provide an HSM audit log entry and internal deletion ticket.
7) Evidence package: audit log snippets (storage deletion ops), KMS receipts, snapshot deletion IDs, API call traces, and estimated timeline for delivery.

Cryptographic sanitization options explained:
- Key deletion (preferred): remove key material from the KMS/HSM. Ciphertexts remain but are irrecoverable. Evidence: key deletion event, KMS audit log entry, key ID, deletion timestamp.
- Crypto-rewrap + zeroization: generate new ephemeral keys, rewrap any remaining ciphertexts (if applicable), then overwrite plaintext caches and run secure-zero on ephemeral volumes. Evidence: rewrap job run logs, zeroization job logs, checksums before/after where supported.
- Physical media procedures (on-prem): overwrite with NIST-recommended patterns or certify drive destruction; provide chain-of-custody and destruction certificate.

Evidence delivery timeline (typical):
- Immediate (within 24 hours): tenant decommission confirmation, list of snapshot/volume IDs scheduled for deletion.
- Short (3-5 business days): storage deletion operation logs, KMS deletion receipts (if performed), and API traces.
- Extended (7-15 business days): consolidated attestation document, signed by Redwood security, and any third-party destruction certificates if applicable.

Attachments: summarized procedure and the exit checklist. If you need stronger SLA language we can add a clause for guaranteed evidence delivery within N business days (subject to enterprise contract).

Let me know which KMS model you plan to use (customer-managed vs Redwood-managed) and whether SecureHealth requires a notarized attestation or a standard signed attestation. We can prepare both templates.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
